# Blockspace Under Pressure: An Analysis of Spam MEV on High-Throughput
Blockchains

Wenhao Wang 
Yale University, IC3 Part of this work was conducted during the Summer 2025
Research Internship at Category Labs. Aditya Saraf11footnotemark: 1 
Cornell University, IC3 Lioba Heimbach 
Category Labs Kushal Babel

Yale University, IC3

###### Abstract

On high-throughput, low-fee blockchains, a qualitatively new form of maximal
extractable value (MEV) has emerged: searchers submit large volumes of
speculative transactions, whose profitability is resolved only at execution
time. We refer to this as _spam MEV_. On major rollups, it can at times
consume more than half of block gas, even though only a small fraction of
probes ultimately results in a trade. Despite growing awareness of this
phenomenon, there is no principled framework for understanding how blockchain
design parameters shape its prevalence and impact.

We develop such a framework, modeling spam transactions competing for on-chain
opportunities under a competitive equilibrium that drives their profits to
zero, and deriving equilibrium spam volumes as a function of block capacity,
minimum gas price, and the transaction fee mechanism. Empirical evidence from
Base and Arbitrum supports the model: spam grew sharply as block capacity was
scaled up and fell when minimum gas prices were introduced. Our analysis
yields three main insights. First, spam is always costly: when block capacity
is scarce, it displaces users and drives up gas prices; as block capacity
grows, it increasingly consumes execution resources, raising network
externality, i.e., the cost of provisioning and processing blocks. We show
that spam takes an increasing share of each additional unit of block capacity,
so capping it before all users are included creates a favorable trade-off:
forgoing a small amount of user welfare eliminates disproportionate spam and
externality. Second, we extend the analysis to priority fee ordering and show
that ordering transactions by gas price helps reduce spam, as spammers must
pay more to reach early block positions. Third, as user demand grows and
blockspace is scaled accordingly, spam s share of block capacity plateaus
rather than growing indefinitely.

## 1 Introduction

Maximal extractable value (MEV) has been a central topic in blockchain
research over the past several years [21, 6, 47]. Much of this work has
focused on the Ethereum Layer 1, which, for a long time, was the primary home
of decentralized finance (DeFi) and thus the main arena for MEV extraction. On
the Ethereum Layer 1, the most widely studied MEV strategies, such as sandwich
attacks, cyclic arbitrage, liquidations, and non-atomic arbitrage, are precise
and targeted: a searcher identifies a specific on-chain opportunity through
off-chain computation, constructs a transaction to capture it, and submits it
with high confidence of success. These strategies rely on the ability to
observe pending transactions in a mempool, i.e., the public waiting area for
transactions awaiting inclusion, or to monitor state changes with sufficient
time to react. Today, competition among searchers on Ethereum is mediated by
block builder auctions [31], in which searchers bid for the right to capture
an opportunity. Only the winning transaction is included on-chain; losing bids
are largely filtered out before execution, keeping most failed MEV attempts
off the blockchain.

A qualitatively different form of MEV has recently emerged on high-throughput,
low-fee blockchains. Rather than targeting a specific opportunity identified
off-chain, searchers submit high volumes of speculative transactions whose
profitability is resolved only at execution time. We refer to this class of
strategies as spam MEV, a term that captures their speculative, high-volume
nature; the phenomenon has also been called _optimistic MEV_ [48] or
_probabilistic MEV_ [40].

In spam MEV, both the detection and execution of opportunities reside largely
in on-chain smart-contract logic [48]: a transaction probes whether a
profitable opportunity exists at the moment of execution and, if so, captures
it. When no opportunity is found, the transaction may revert or simply consume
gas, i.e., the computational cost of executing transactions on the blockchain,
searching without ever executing a trade. This encompasses a range of
speculative strategies, though cyclic arbitrage is the most prominently
studied among them. To illustrate the contrast: as studied on the Ethereum
Layer 1, a cyclic arbitrage bot precomputes a profitable path and executes a
single atomic transaction, whereas on many high-throughput chains, the same
type of bot speculatively submits transactions without knowing if an
opportunity exists, repeatedly probing liquidity pools in the hope of
capturing small gains and accepting a high failure rate in exchange for
marginal profits.

First documented on Solana [53], spam MEV has since been identified on
Ethereum Layer 2 rollups, including Base, Optimism, and Arbitrum [48, 30]. The
scale of the phenomenon is striking: on Base and Optimism, spam MEV
transactions consumed over 50% of block gas in Q1 2025 [48], yet only 6 12% of
these speculative probes result in an actual trade. On top of that, despite
consuming more than half of on-chain gas, spam MEV transactions pay less than
a quarter of total fees [48], as they carry low priority fees.

What makes spam MEV viable and prevalent? A combination of architectural and
economic features common to modern high-throughput chains likely plays a role.
Low transaction fees reduce the cost of failed speculative transactions,
making repeated probing profitable even at low success rates. Fast block
times, often below one second on rollups, can leave insufficient time for
searchers to observe state changes and submit targeted transactions before the
next block is produced, favoring continuous speculative submission over
deliberate off-chain computation. Similarly, most high-throughput chains lack
a public mempool, e.g., rollups use centralized sequencers and Solana forwards
transactions directly to the current block producer, limiting the information
available for targeted extraction. Designs such as encrypted mempools [3, 7,
25], when deployed, are likely to only increase spam MEV by further reducing
the information available for targeted MEV strategies.

While the prevalence of spam MEV has been documented, there is no principled
framework to study the interplay between design parameters and spam volumes,
and the impact of spam on various stakeholders. As a result, the response from
various blockchain designers has been largely reactive and ad-hoc (c.f.
Section 1.1).

In this work, we fill this gap by developing a framework to determine the
equilibrium volume of spam as a result of blockspace and fee design choices,
and to analyze the impact of resulting spam on three fronts: (1) user welfare,
(2) validator revenue, and (3) network externality, i.e., the cost of
provisioning block capacity and processing transactions.We characterize the
tradeoffs involved in design choices and provide guidance for blockchain
designers to navigate these tradeoffs.

In the remainder of this section, we first highlight the industry s response
to the rise of spam MEV, describe the design levers and metrics we focus on in
this work, and then summarize our contributions.

### 1.1 Ecosystem Response

The prevalence of spam MEV has not gone unnoticed. The blockchain community
has become increasingly aware of the scale of the problem, and a debate has
emerged about how harmful spam truly is and what should be done about it.
Flashbots  thesis that MEV fundamentally limits scaling [41], i.e., that added
throughput capacity is absorbed by spam rather than passed on to genuine
users, has been particularly influential in framing the discussion.

The most visible case study is Base, the Ethereum Layer 2 rollup with the
highest DeFi total value locked (TVL) [22]. Following the Dencun upgrade,
which drastically reduced Layer 2 data availability costs, Base increased its
block gas limit. However, the additional capacity was largely consumed by spam
MEV rather than benefiting genuine users [48, 30]. As Figure 1(a) shows, spam
gas grew disproportionately faster than non-spam gas as Base progressively
raised its gas target after Dencun, absorbing the majority of the added
capacity. When the community took notice [48, 30, 41], Base reduced the gas
target from 70M to 50M. Figure 1(b) shows that comparing the 30 days before
and after the change, spam gas fell by 34% and non-spam gas by 24%, i.e., both
declined but spam absorbed a larger share of the reduction. Beyond blockspace
consumption, spam also imposes costs on the broader network infrastructure.
Multiple blockchain indexing services, including Etherscan, announced they
would discontinue free API access for Base, citing the significant
infrastructure costs driven by the high transaction volumes [36, 35, 24]. Base
ultimately raised its minimum transaction fee, explicitly citing spam
reduction as the rationale [8]. As Figure 2(a) shows, spam gas on Base trended
downward over this period, coinciding with successive increases in the
protocol minimum gas price, though other factors may have also contributed.

Arbitrum, the rollup with the second-highest DeFi TVL [22], had set a minimum
gas price meaningfully above the physical minimum of 1 wei before the recent
wave of attention on spam, and notably experienced significantly less spam
than other rollups throughout 2025, though still more than the Ethereum Layer

overhaul [57, 5]. As Figure 2(b) shows, spam gas dipped briefly in the first
weeks after the change but then surged well above pre-change levels due to a
single new player that entered (c.f. Section 7). Outside the EVM ecosystem,
Aptos also announced an increase to its minimum gas fee [4].

Newer chains have launched with spam in mind: Monad, for instance, sets a non-
trivial minimum gas price and charges transactions based on the gas limit
rather than gas consumed, making speculative transactions with large unused
gas allocations more costly [16].

These interventions share a common intuition: spam imposes costs on the
network, and the costs of curtailing it are worth bearing. Yet the responses
have been largely reactive and chain-specific, without formal analysis of how
design parameters interact to determine the equilibrium level of spam. A key
factor is that, unlike Ethereum L1 where congestion pricing naturally emerges,
high-throughput chains can have slack capacity where the market-clearing gas
price approaches zero, while the network still bears the cost of processing
every transaction. A minimum gas price gming_{\text{min}} ensures that each
transaction pays at least a meaningful contribution toward its marginal cost
and, as our analysis shows, serves as a key lever against spam in this regime.

### 1.2 Design Levers

We now describe the blockchain design choices that may influence spam
transactions. These are the parameters that our framework analyzes.

Block Space Limit BmaxB_{\text{max}}. The block space limit affects inclusion
costs. When the limit BmaxB_{\text{max}} is low relative to transaction
demand, competition for inclusion in the block intensifies, increasing gas
prices gg and may therefore reduce the expected revenue of each spam
transaction. Conversely, when BmaxB_{\text{max}} is large enough to
accommodate all transactions, gas prices gg decrease, and therefore increase
the expected profit of spam transactions.

Minimum Gas Price gming_{\text{min}}. A blockchain can impose a minimum gas
price gming_{\text{min}} per transaction, independent of block space
availability. Higher values of gming_{\text{min}} increase the cost when block
capacity is slack, influencing the economic outcome for both spam and non-spam
transactions. In the absence of a price floor, the equilibrium gas price gg
would approach zero when block capacity exceeds demand, resulting in a
disproportionately high volume of spam transactions.

Transaction Fee Mechanism. The design of the transaction fee mechanism (TFM)
impacts transaction submission behavior. Spam transactions often specify a
large gas limit but typically consume only a fraction of it when executed
without profitable arbitrage opportunities [48]. A TFM that imposes higher
costs for specifying large unused gas limits can alter transaction submission
strategies. Additionally, a TFM can dictate the ordering of transactions
within a block, such as through priority fee ordering, which affects the
resulting spam volumes.

### 1.3 Our Framework and Contributions

We develop a framework for analyzing spam MEV and the interplay with
blockchain design choices. We model spam bots as actors competing among
themselves for opportunities on-chain, and study how the resulting equilibrium
spam volume depends on the block space limit BmaxB_{\text{max}}, the minimum
gas price gming_{\text{min}}, and the transaction fee mechanism. We measure
the impact of spam along three dimensions: _user welfare_ (aggregate surplus
of users), _validator revenue_ (total fees collected from all transactions),
and _network externality_ (the cost borne by the network for provisioning
block capacity and processing transactions). These metrics are formally
defined in Section 2 along with our model for user demand, TFM and users  and
spam bots  utility. Our main results are:

 1. 1.

Closed-form equilibrium spam volume and gas prices (Section 3.1): The
equilibrium spam volume takes one of three forms: (1) no profitable entry for
spam transactions, (2) an equilibrium determined entirely by
gming_{\text{min}} when slack blockspace is available and spam does not
interfere with or crowd out other users, or (3) a congested equilibrium given
by a closed-form expression. The three regimes are clearly characterized based
on block capacity BmaxB_{\text{max}}. The equilibrium gas price remains at
gming_{\text{min}} in the second scenario, and is driven up by spam only in
the third scenario.

 2. 2.

User welfare, revenue and externality characterization along with trade-offs
(Section 3.2): We analyze these metrics in equilibrium and characterize the
trade-off regions between user welfare on one side, and revenue and
externality on the other side. We study the loss in user welfare (and increase
in revenue and externality) compared to a baseline world where no spam exists.
The loss in welfare is maximized when block capacity exactly equals the
quantity demanded by users at the floor price gming_{\text{min}}, where spam
causes maximum displacement. We show that the design parameters where users
are most harmed by spam is also where the network s revenue gain from spam is
largest.

 3. 3.

Parameter-setting guidance (Section 3.3): We characterize the joint choice of
(Bmax,gmin)(B_{\text{max}},g_{\text{min}}), showing that the effective ceiling
on useful block capacity is BplatB_{\mathrm{plat}} and that the optimal
strategy depends on the tradeoff between user welfare and network externality.
We show that as blockspace is scaled, spam consumes an increasing proportion
of the marginal capacity added. Consequently, we give precise guidance on
setting design parameters that significantly reduce spam at the cost of
relatively small reduction in user welfare (due to low-value users).

 4. 4.

Priority fee ordering (Section 4): We extend our theoretical analysis to an
approximate priority fee ordering (PFO) TFM where blocks are divided into sub-
blocks ordered by gas prices, with ordering in each sub-block being random. We
show that priority ordering reduces spam by making early block placement
expensive, and compute the equilibrium spam volume and outcome metrics.

 5. 5.

Demand-scaling analysis (Section 5 and Section 7): We tackle the question of
whether and to what extent does spam pose a limit to scaling [41]. We first
use real-world data from Base and Arbitrum to estimate the relationship
between rise in MEV opportunity and increase in non-spam volume, finding it to
be approximately linear. We then show that when user demand grows and
blockspace is scaled accordingly, spam does not vanish or explode: it remains
a nontrivial share of included gas. Priority fee ordering lowers this share,
but does not eliminate it.

 6. 6.

Mitigations (Section 6): We draw insights from our analysis to propose
practical mitigations for regimes where spam poses a concern. We divide our
mitigations into two families: (1) incentive-based mechanisms (gas price
floors, charging transactions based on the gas they reserve, i.e., gas-limit,
rather than gas-used) and what we call cheap-path mechanisms that skip or
cheaply execute the spam that does make it on-chain. The cheap path methods
include filtering by the block producer if execution is not the bottleneck,
and providing cancellation mechanisms in case execution is the bottleneck.

 7. 7.

Empirical evidence and case studies (Section 7): Finally, we present empirical
case studies of spam volumes on Base and Arbitrum over the period of January
2024 February 2026. This period is particularly interesting as these
blockchains experimented with various parameter choices for minimum gas price
and block capacity. We study the relationship between spam volumes (along with
non-spam volumes) and the design levers in our framework. We show that our
empirical findings agree with several predictions from our theoretical model:
(1) spam volume reduces when a minimum price floor is introduced or increased,
with non-spam throughput remaining stable; (2) spam volume increases when
block capacity is increased; (3) spam consumes a disproportionate share of the
marginal blockspace as more blockspace is added; and (4) on Base spam is
concentrated toward later positions in the block, matching the prediction of
our PFO model.

## 2 Model

We present our model for analyzing spam MEV. The design levers (block space
limit BmaxB_{\text{max}}, minimum gas price gming_{\text{min}}, and
transaction fee mechanism) were introduced in Section 1.2. For our transaction
fee mechanism, we choose a mechanism that charges a transaction for its gas
limit rather than gas used, and blockspace is counted in terms of transaction
gas limits, similar to high-throughput blockchains such as Solana and Monad
[16]. This has the effect of gas charge being independent of actual execution,
but our results can be straightforwardly adapted to a mechanism that charges
only for the used gas (c.f. discussion in Section 6). For our initial analysis
in Section 3, the TFM orders transactions in a random order, mimicking the
operations of a low-latency blockchain. We extend our analysis to priority-fee
based ordering in Section 4.

### 2.2 Metrics

We now describe the metrics used to quantify the impact of spam transactions
on the blockchain.

###### Definition 2.1 (User Welfare).

The user welfare is defined as the aggregate utility of all users, i.e., the
sum of ui fiu_{i}-f_{i} across all included users. As shown in Fig. 3 for a
linear demand curve, the user welfare is the area under the demand curve above
the clearing price g g^{*}. A higher user welfare indicates a greater overall
benefit to users of the blockchain. We note that in our analysis in the
following sections, user welfare is essentially the social welfare of all
blockchain transaction senders, including the senders of the spam
transactions, since in the equilibrium case the expected utility of each spam
transaction is zero.

###### Definition 2.2 (Validator Revenue).

Validator revenue is the total gas fees collected from all included
transactions (both users and spammers), written as R=g BR=g^{*}\cdot B, where
g g^{*} is the equilibrium clearing gas price and BB is total gas used. This
quantity is _strictly positive_ and represents the direct income to the
network from transaction processing. For the purposes of this work, we do not
consider burning of fees or block rewards, as they are merely a way to change
allocation of revenue between token holders and validators, and do not affect
the net economic incentives for spamming or the overall welfare analysis.

###### Definition 2.3 (Network Externality).

The network externality is the cost borne by the network for provisioning
block capacity and processing transactions, written as

## 4 Analysis with (Approximate) Priority Fee Ordering

We now turn to a TFM with priority fee ordering (PFO), where transactions are
executed in decreasing order of their bids rather than randomly. This is
promising for reducing spam, as in the random-ordering model, spam
transactions can occupy early positions in the block without paying more than
others, whereas under PFO, such placement becomes costly.

To capture the effects of PFO, we analyze a tractable approximation that
extends the random-ordering model in Section 3. Concretely, we assume that the
block is divided into nn sub-blocks of equal capacity. These sub-blocks
represent increasingly late execution positions in the block. Transactions
that choose to pay for priority are sorted into these sub-blocks by their
priority bids, with higher bids placed earlier. Within each sub-block,
however, the order of transactions is still random. Each transaction in a
priority sub-block pays the minimum price required for inclusion in that sub-
block.

For example, if n=2n=2, then priority transactions with higher bids are placed
in the first sub-block and are executed before priority transactions in the
second sub-block. Transactions that do not compete for priority are placed
only after all priority transactions, in the lowest occupied part of the
block. They all pay the minimum fee needed to be included in the block, rather
than the higher price needed to obtain an earlier execution slot.

In general, the block therefore consists of two regions. The upper region is
priority-ordered: transactions there are divided across sub-blocks according
to their priority bids, and higher-priority sub-blocks execute first. The
lower region is inclusion-only: transactions there do not compete for earlier
execution and instead pay the common minimum inclusion price for the block.
The rest of the model stays the same. In particular, we still assume that the
opportunity is randomly and independently located among the included user gas.

To capture the fact that not all users wish to compete for priority, we assume
that a fraction v [0,1]v\in[0,1] of users opt into the priority market, while
the remaining fraction 1 v1-v seek only inclusion. Users always bid honestly
relative to their chosen service class. Priority-seeking users bid according
to their willingness to pay for earlier execution, while inclusion-only users
submit the minimum price needed to enter the block.

Let g \bar{g} denote the minimum price needed for inclusion in the block,
i.e., the clearing price of the last occupied sub-block. Conditional on this
g \bar{g}, the demand of priority-seeking users is
DT (g )=v D (g ),D^{\mathrm{T}}(\bar{g})=vD(\bar{g}), while the demand of
inclusion-only users is
DL (g )=(1 v) D (g ).D^{\mathrm{L}}(\bar{g})=(1-v)D(\bar{g}). Thus, only the
v D (g )vD(\bar{g}) priority-seeking users contribute to the price ladder
across earlier sub-blocks. The remaining (1 v) D (g )(1-v)D(\bar{g}) users
appear only in the lowest-price occupied part of the block, and all of them
pay the common inclusion price g \bar{g}.

Spam bots are modeled analogously. A spam attempt can either compete for an
earlier execution position or seek inclusion only. In our approximate model, a
spam transaction assigned to sub-block ii should therefore be interpreted as a
spam bid just high enough to obtain the execution priority of that sub-block.
This lets the equilibrium endogenously determine how much spam enters the
expensive priority region and how much remains in the low-price inclusion
region.

Finally, like in the previous section, we assume that the opportunity value

### 4.1 Competitive spam equilibrium

In a competitive equilibrium, the utility of spam within each sub-block is
zero, similar to Section 3. This lets us compute equilibrium spam volume
iteratively, from the top sub-block downward. In the interest of space, we
defer the detailed steps to derive the equilibrium to Section B.1.

Figure 8 shows that PFO (with n=500n=500 sub-blocks) reduces spam volume

comes from the price separation it creates across sub-blocks. When vv is
large, PFO reduces spam relative to the random-ordering benchmark, because
early sub-blocks become expensive and spammers must pay more to place
transactions near the top of the block. As more users compete for priority,
the price gap between early and late sub-blocks becomes larger, which makes it
harder for spammers to spread attempts across the block and lowers the spam
volume.

At the same time, the figure also shows that PFO does not always reduce spam.
In particular, when v=0v=0, spam can be higher than under random ordering. We
note that this should be read mainly as an artifact of our approximate PFO
model. The reason is that sub-blocks give spammers more control over where to
place their attempts. Even if early sub-blocks contain no spam, it is still
profitable to place spam in the last sub-block, since those transactions can
capture opportunities that survive from earlier parts of the block while
paying only the lower inclusion price of the last sub-block. By contrast, in
the random-ordering case, first-unit entry may fail to be profitable
altogether when the opportunity value is too small relative to the single
clearing price. Thus, PFO helps only when enough user demand is actually
competing for priority.

Takeaway (Priority fee ordering). Priority fee ordering is effective at
reducing spam when many users pay for priority. When few do, most occupied
sub-blocks clear at the common inclusion price g \bar{g}, leaving spammers
with relatively cheap access to early execution slots.

## 6 Mitigations to Spam

Our theoretical analysis highlights that spam transactions consume block space
yet produce essentially no state changes. In the model, this appears as a
reduction in useful block space, meaning less gas is left for non-spam users,
which lowers user welfare. This motivates mitigations that do not treat spam
as a binary  attack  to be eliminated, but instead as a form of _resource
abuse_ : most spam transactions consume resources without producing useful
output.

This view also matches what we see in practice. Even when spam is not a
consensus safety threat, sustained no-effect traffic can still create real
operational pressure on RPC providers, indexers, and explorers, and some
infrastructure operators have publicly downgraded support during spam on Base
[36, 35, 24]. At the protocol and client level, multiple ecosystems (including
Base, Aptos, and Arbitrum) have responded by making low-value traffic more
expensive via fee floors or minimum gas budgets, which can be interpreted as a
simple incentive-based mechanism against high-volume probing [8, 57, 5, 4].

We organize mitigations into two families. The first family makes probing more
expensive at the margin so that competitive entry yields less spam volume,
which we call _incentive-based mechanisms_. The second family accepts that
spam will exist, but tries to make failed probes cheaper to process than full
on-chain execution, which we call _cheap-path mechanisms_. We note that in
practice, one can combine approaches in both families.

### 6.1 Incentive-based mechanisms

Incentive-based mechanisms reduce spam by increasing the expected cost of
(failed) spam transactions, so that in the equilibrium, fewer spam attempts
are sent to the blockchain. These mechanisms do not require perfectly
identifying spam, and they can be deployed as coarse policies that target the
main source of externality, which is resource consumption.

Minimum gas prices. A simple mechanism is to set a nontrivial floor gas price
(i.e., increasing gming_{\text{min}}). As discussed in Section 1.1, several
chains have adopted nontrivial fee floors, some from launch and others in
response to observed spam [8, 57, 5, 4, 50]. This is consistent with our
analysis in Section 3: a sufficiently high floor gas price caps spam volume
and preserves useful block space for users. We provide empirical evidence for
this effect in Section 7.

Charging for reserved execution gas. Another deterrence lever is to charge
based on _gas limit_ rather than ex post gas used. This directly targets spam
strategies that intentionally revert early or do minimal work when they fail.
In our model (Section 3), this changes the cost of each attempt from  pay only
when you win  toward  pay for the capacity you force others to keep
available , which reduces equilibrium spam volume. Monad, for instance,
adopted this approach [16].

### 6.2 Cheap-path mechanisms

Cheap-path mechanisms aim to keep the cost borne by the system from failed
spam transactions much smaller than the cost of regularly executing them on-
chain. The design choice depends on whether execution is the bottleneck for
the block producer, i.e., the sequencer on a rollup or validators on Layer-1.
If execution is not the bottleneck, the block producer can afford to spend
extra work on simulation and filtering. If execution is the bottleneck, the
design should instead avoid executing failed spam transactions altogether.

Filtering when execution is not the bottleneck. When the block producer can
simulate transactions off the critical path, it can filter out those that
produce no state changes before including them in a block. On Ethereum,
builders and relays already simulate candidate transactions as part of the
MEV-Boost pipeline [28], and enshrined proposer-builder separation would make
this role explicit at the protocol level [13]. On rollups, the centralized
sequencer can similarly simulate the ordered stream and drop no-effect
transactions before posting data to Layer 1, saving data availability costs.
Unichain, for instance, implements revert protection: the sequencer simulates
transactions and excludes those that would revert, so users do not pay gas for
failed attempts [54]. A practical concern is that these block producers
themselves become targets for spam, as searchers flood them with candidate
transactions to simulate. Reputation systems, rate limits, or even out-of-band
transaction fees at the block producer level can mitigate this, similar to the
operational protections that relays already implement today [28]. A further
design constraint is auditability: third parties must be able to verify that
the block producer did not selectively drop valid transactions under the guise
of filtering.

Cancellation when execution is the bottleneck. When execution resources are
scarce, the more direct approach is to allow a failed spam transaction to be
cancelled without executing it fully, provided the cancellation is justified
in a verifiable way. One possible design is a proof-carrying cancellation
rule, where the sender (or a third-party prover) provides evidence that the
transaction would lead to no state changes, and the system charges a smaller
but nonzero fee. Because per-transaction verification (e.g., using ZKP) can be
expensive when failed probes are short, a practical variant batches many  no-
effect  proofs into a single aggregate proof per block or per sender,
amortizing verification while still charging per cancelled attempt for its gas
usage.

## 7 Empirical Analysis

Our previous analysis predicts that spam absorbs a disproportionate share of
marginal block capacity (BmaxB_{\text{max}}) and that the gas price floor
(gming_{\text{min}}) directly gates spam profitability. We now examine how
these two design levers affect spam in practice by analyzing daily spam gas on
two major Ethereum Layer 2 rollups, Base and Arbitrum, which have undergone
significant changes to both parameters during our observation period.

### 7.1 Data and methodology

We collect 790 daily observations per chain from January 2024 through February
2026 using Dune Analytics. To classify spam, we use an approach similar to the
methodology employed by Flashbots [41] and consistent with the optimistic
probing behavior described by Solmaz et al. [48]: we identify contracts that
interact with decentralized exchanges (DEXes) but frequently fail to execute
trades, i.e., they probe for arbitrage opportunities without producing ERC-20
token transfers. Using on-chain traces, we find all transactions where a
contract makes an internal call to a known DEX pool or router address. For
each such transaction, we check whether it produced at least one ERC-20
transfer event. Contracts that interact with DEXes but produce no token
transfer are probing but not trading. For each contract and month, we compute
the fraction of DEX-interacting transactions that produced a transfer.
Contracts with a transfer rate below 50% and at least 10 interactions are
classified as spam candidates. We rank candidates by total gas consumed and
conservatively retain only the top 100 per month. We then attribute all daily
transactions from these contracts to spam transactions. Non-spam gas is the
total gas minus spam gas.

### 7.5 Summary

Spam scales super-linearly with block capacity (elasticity of 2.27) and
disproportionately fills marginal capacity. Reducing the gas target reduces
spam but also reduces non-spam throughput. The minimum gas price affects the
two types of gas differently: on Base, the gas price floor steps that reduced
spam did so while non-spam gas remained stable or grew. On Arbitrum, the fee
doubling did not produce a lasting reduction, possibly because the increase
was too small relative to spam profitability. These patterns are consistent
with our theoretical analysis: when fees are low and capacity is abundant,
increasing the gas price floor or reducing capacity can significantly gate
spam without compromising non-spam throughput, corroborating the mitigation
mechanisms discussed in Section 6.

## 8 Related Work

Empirics of spam MEV. Spam MEV was first documented on Solana by Umbra
Research [53], who observed high failure rates among MEV transactions and
provided early evidence that high-throughput, low-fee chains incentivize
redundant submissions over priority-fee competition. Solmaz et al. [48] study
optimistic cyclic arbitrage patterns on Ethereum Layer 2 rollups and find that
cyclic arbitrage bots consumed over 50% of gas on Base and Optimism by early
2025, with only 6 12% of probes resulting in a trade. Gogol et al. [30] study
reverted transactions on five rollups, finding that revert rates rose sharply
after Dencun; by restricting to reverts, they capture one subtype of spam
implementation and strategy, as not all unsuccessful probes revert. These
works are primarily empirical. Our work develops a framework that
characterizes how block capacity, gas price floors, and the transaction fee
mechanism jointly determine spam volume, and analyzes the resulting impact on
user welfare, validator revenue, and network externality. We complement the
analysis with empirical evidence from Base and Arbitrum.

Modeling spam MEV. Concurrent with our work, Mazorra et al. [40] model spam as
a timing game among a finite number of searchers competing for an opportunity,
showing that timing competition fully dissipates expected profits. Their
equilibrium spam volume in the large-nn limit corresponds exactly to ours,
despite the models being derived independently. The two models are
complementary: Mazorra et al. characterize when and how often each searcher
submits in the timing game, while we focus on how protocol design parameters,
i.e., block capacity, gas price floors, and transaction ordering, jointly
shape spam volume and its welfare and externality implications.

In related work, Capponi and Zhu [15] model costly duplicate submissions as a
latency race among traders competing for time-sensitive opportunities on
blockchains, framing the problem as an observable analogue of HFT latency
investment. They show that a time-priority auction (Timeboost) reduces
redundant submissions and reallocates the waste into platform revenue, and
validate this prediction on Arbitrum using a difference-in-differences design.
Their focus is on a specific auction mechanism as mitigation, whereas we study
how general design parameters, i.e., block capacity, gas price floors, and
transaction ordering, jointly shape spam volume and welfare.

Targeted MEV. Eskandari et al. [23] taxonomized front-running attacks on
Ethereum, and Daian et al. [21] broadened the scope to MEV more generally,
documenting priority gas auctions among searchers. Qin et al. [47] and Torres
et al. [51] subsequently quantified sandwich attacks, arbitrage, and
liquidations at scale. A large body of further work has measured specific
strategies and infrastructure on the Ethereum Layer 1 [62, 60, 32, 56, 58, 46,
1, 63, 55, 31], on alternative Layer 1s [44], and across chains and rollups
[52, 29, 45, 43]. These works study targeted MEV, i.e., strategies where
searchers identify a specific opportunity off-chain and submit a transaction
to capture it. Our work, in contrast, focuses on spam MEV, where searchers
submit speculative transactions whose profitability is resolved only at
execution time.

MEV prevention. Proposed mitigations for targeted MEV include protocol-
specific parameter tuning [33, 61], trusted third-party ordering via relays or
private mempools [20, 26, 27, 19], fair ordering protocols [38, 37, 39, 14],
commit reveal and privacy-preserving schemes [59, 42, 11], trusted execution
environments [9, 49], and encrypted mempools via threshold encryption [17, 18,
2, 3, 10, 7]; see Heimbach and Wattenhofer [34] for a comprehensive
systematization. Spam MEV, however, is largely unaddressed by these mechanisms
and may even be worsened: encrypted mempools, for instance, remove the
information advantage that enables targeted extraction, potentially shifting
searchers toward speculative, high-volume strategies instead. As part of this
work, we also propose mitigations specifically targeting spam MEV.

## 9 Conclusions and Future Directions

We develop a framework for analyzing spam MEV under a competitive equilibrium,
deriving equilibrium spam volumes and characterizing the impact on user
welfare, validator revenue, and network externality. Empirical evidence from
Base and Arbitrum validates our predictions.

Three main insights emerge. First, spam always imposes a cost: through reduced
user welfare when block capacity is tight, through increased network
externality when capacity is abundant, or both. We show that spam claims a
growing share of each marginal unit of block capacity; consequently, capping
block capacity slightly below BplatB_{\mathrm{plat}} yields a favorable trade-
off: a modest welfare reduction removes a disproportionate amount of spam and
substantially lowers externality. Second, priority fee ordering helps curb
spam by requiring spammers to bid more for earlier block positions. Third,
under demand scaling, spam does not capture an ever-larger fraction of
blockspace but instead settles at a bounded share.

An important direction for future work is the broader design of mechanisms
that reduce the cost of spam without harming legitimate users. This includes
both making spam less attractive to send and making failed probes cheaper for
the system to process. Understanding how these approaches interact and perform
across different blockchain architectures remains an open question.

## Appendix D MEV Revenue Scaling with User Volume

In this appendix, we estimate how the opportunity value rr scales with user
demand in deployed systems. This matters for the scaling analysis in the main
text. If MEV opportunity size grows with user activity, then the amount of
spam that can be sustained at equilibrium may also grow with adoption.

#### Methodology.

We study cyclic arbitrage on Ethereum Layer 2 rollups. Our main case study is
Base, and we also report corresponding estimates for Arbitrum. We use daily
observations and identify cyclic arbitrage transactions from decoded DEX swap
data on Dune Analytics. A transaction is classified as cyclic arbitrage if it
contains at least three swaps that form a cycle, meaning that the first token
sold is also the last token bought, and the transaction yields a positive net
balance in exactly that token. We exclude transactions routed through known
DEX aggregator contracts, since these are more likely to reflect user-
initiated routing rather than MEV. For each arbitrage transaction, we compute
gross profit from the net token balance and subtract the gas fee to obtain net
profit. We then aggregate these net profits by day and use the resulting daily
total as a proxy for the available opportunity value rr. This proxy is
imperfect, but it is natural in a competitive setting, since realized
arbitrage profits should track the amount of extractable value available to
searchers.

estimate the log-log regression
